title: Bollywood Takes Over BRICS: Anwar Ibrahim and an Indonesian Journalist Sing Hindi Classics in Delhi
excerpt: The Malaysian prime minister sang a Kishore Kumar classic at a BRICS gala dinner while an Indonesian journalist performed a 1990s hit — as serious diplomacy, including an upgraded India-Malaysia partnership, moved forward offstage.
body:
• Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim sang Kishore Kumar's 1965 classic "Khwab Ho Tum Ya Koi Haqeeqat" at a BRICS gala dinner in New Delhi, accompanied by a live pianist.
  • An Indonesian journalist also broke into the 1990 hit "Jab Koi Baat Bigad Jaye" at the summit, making Bollywood the unofficial soundtrack of the 18th BRICS Summit.
  • Anwar's visit also produced serious diplomacy: India and Malaysia elevated ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership with new pacts on digital technology and tourism.
  • The musical moments reflect a growing pattern of Bollywood being used as soft-power diplomacy at major summits.

The 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi had its share of weighty communiques and closed-door meetings, but two of its most talked-about moments involved neither trade nor geopolitics. They involved Bollywood songs. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim sang a Kishore Kumar classic at a gala dinner, while an Indonesian journalist broke into a 1990s romantic anthem at the summit — turning India's signature cultural export into the unofficial language of the summit.

A Prime Minister at the Piano

Anwar Ibrahim, who is visiting India for the BRICS Summit on his first trip to the country since becoming Malaysia's prime minister in 2022, performed Kishore Kumar's "Khwab Ho Tum Ya Koi Haqeeqat" at a gala dinner in the capital. Accompanied by a live pianist, he sang the track from the 1965 film Teen Devian, composed by S.D. Burman with lyrics by Majrooh Sultanpuri.

https://x.com/TimesNow/status/2099015975538704390

Video of the performance was posted to Anwar's own X account, where it spread quickly across Indian social media. According to ANI, the rendition blended statecraft with classic Bollywood melody and reflected a long-standing personal appreciation for Hindi cinema that surfaces frequently during Anwar's diplomatic engagements.

His taste for Bollywood is well documented. During an earlier diplomatic exchange with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Anwar shared an official video montage set to "Bole Chudiyan" from Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham. He has also performed "Dost Dost Na Raha" during previous India visits, according to WION.

"See, Prime Minister Modi is so popular; I got so many messages to pass on regards to him."

— Anwar Ibrahim, Prime Minister of Malaysia

The musical moment sat alongside substantive diplomacy. Anwar's visit yielded the elevation of India-Malaysia bilateral ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, with multiple pacts signed covering digital technology and tourism cooperation. On the sidelines of the summit, he held bilateral talks with Modi on trade, investment, defence, semiconductors, infrastructure, digital economy, energy, education and people-to-people ties. He also praised India's civilisational heritage and expressed optimism that outstanding issues between India and Pakistan would find a peaceful resolution.

A Journalist Joins In

Anwar was not the only visitor to find a microphone at the summit. An Indonesian journalist covering the BRICS proceedings sang "Jab Koi Baat Bigad Jaye," the 1990 classic from the film Jurm sung by Kumar Sanu and Sadhana Sargam, according to NDTV. The performance added to a string of Bollywood moments involving Indonesian visitors: in January 2025, an Indonesian delegation sang "Kuch Kuch Hota Hai" at a banquet hosted by President Droupadi Murmu in honour of Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto at Rashtrapati Bhavan.

Indonesia joined BRICS as a full member in January 2025, while Malaysia became one of its partner countries the same month — giving both nations a fresh stage at the Delhi summit.

Bollywood as Diplomacy

None of this is accidental. Bollywood has long been one of India's most potent exports — its films dominate screens and streaming queues from Kuala Lumpur to Jakarta, and Hindi film songs are staples at weddings and celebrations across Southeast Asia. When a visiting head of government sings a Kishore Kumar number, it registers in a way that a tariff negotiation never can.

The summit itself, themed around building resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability, produced the New Delhi Declaration and wide-ranging discussions on development and global governance. But the songs may be what ordinary people remember — and in diplomacy, that kind of warmth is a currency of its own.

What to Watch

Watch for the summit's final outcomes on economic cooperation and institutional reform, and for whether the India-Malaysia partnership's new pacts on digital technology and tourism translate into concrete projects. As for the music: the videos are already circulating, and the next summit has a high bar for impromptu performances.
